title: Thou art the man (2 Samuel 11–12)
hook: adultery, murder, and a prophet's story that makes the king see himself

segments.voice: Yesterday, David dancing before the ark with all his might. Your line was dance anyway. Where did you let your joy show? Today, the same king at his lowest. Day four hundred five.

It's spring, the text says, the season when kings go out to war. David sends his army out and stays home. One afternoon he gets up from his bed, walks on the palace roof, and sees a woman bathing. He asks who she is. Bathsheba, Bethsabee in the Douay-Rheims, the wife of Uriah, one of his own soldiers, away at the front. David sends for her. He's the king; nobody refuses the king. She becomes pregnant. To hide it, David brings Uriah home, but the loyal soldier won't sleep in comfort while his comrades are in tents. So David writes a letter, has Uriah carry it himself, and it says: put him at the front, and pull back.
screen: `THE KING STAYS HOME FROM WAR.` → `A WOMAN SEEN FROM THE ROOF.` → `A LETTER CARRIED BY ITS VICTIM.`

segments.voice: Uriah dies. David marries Bathsheba. Everything looks handled. Then God sends the prophet Nathan, and Nathan doesn't accuse. He tells a story. Two men in one city. One rich, with flocks and herds. One poor, with nothing but one little ewe lamb, which, the Douay says, grew up with his children, ate from his plate, drank from his cup, slept in his arms, and "was unto him as a daughter." A traveler comes to visit the rich man, and the rich man doesn't take from his own flocks. He takes the poor man's lamb and serves it for dinner. David is furious. The man who did this deserves to die! He'll pay it back four times over! And Nathan says four words: "Thou art the man." That's how the story works. David could see the injustice clearly as long as it was somebody else. The parable gets past his defenses, and then turns around. And here's what sets David apart from so many powerful men in history: he doesn't kill the prophet. He doesn't spin it. He says, "I have sinned against the Lord." Nathan answers: the Lord hath taken away thy sin. The consequences still come; the chapters ahead are full of grief in David's house. But the forgiveness is real. Tradition gives this moment a song. The Douay's Psalm fifty, the Miserere, has a heading that sets it here, when Nathan came to David. It begins: "Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy." The Church prays it constantly, and many Catholics know its spirit from the confessional: say it plainly, and be forgiven.
screen: `NATHAN TELLS A STORY.` · `THE POOR MAN'S LITTLE EWE LAMB.` · `I HAVE SINNED AGAINST THE LORD.` · `THE MISERERE: HAVE MERCY ON ME.` · then, large: `THOU ART THE MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let a friend tell you a hard truth. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people who could be your Nathan, the ones who'd tell you the truth to your face. Now ask what they might say if you gave them permission. Is there a pattern you can spot in others and not in yourself? Sit with the possibility without arguing. If you pray, you can say the first words of the Miserere: have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy. Then think about who you'll ask, this week, to be honest with you. The bell holds the time.
Thou art the man. Nathan's four words to King David, turning a story about someone else into a mirror, and leading the king to confess. Today's word.
Your line: thou art the man. Today, when you feel outrage at someone else's wrong, ask once whether the story is also about you. Day four hundred five.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 51 (50 in the Douay numbering), the Miserere, at Morning Prayer on Fridays in the Liturgy of the Hours, and many use it to prepare for the sacrament of confession.

fork.setup: you're King David. a prophet has just tricked you into condemning yourself, in front of your court. you're the most powerful man in Israel. what do you do?
options: explain that kings live by different rules.
admit it: I have sinned against the Lord.
fork.reveal: David confesses, and Nathan says the Lord has taken away his sin. the consequences still come, but the king's first move is honesty.

original.note: Hebrew: I have sinned. In the Hebrew, David's whole confession to Nathan is just two words.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scandal story about a king and a bathing woman.
what it means: power, adultery and murder, undone by a prophet's story that makes the king see himself, and a confession without excuses.
what a scholar hears: in Hebrew David's confession is two words, chatati la-YHWH; and Psalm 51's heading ties the Miserere to this very moment.

notes: Bathsheba's part is told carefully: the text gives her no words before 11:5, and David holds the power ('nobody refuses the king' is interpretive). Confirm the Keeper is comfortable with this framing.
'Kings go forth to war' in spring: the Douay says 'at the return of the year'; 'spring' is a common gloss. Confirm.
Psalm 51 (Douay 50) at Friday Morning Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours (four-week psalter): confirm.
David's confession is two Hebrew words (chatati la-YHWH); 'just two words' counts chatati plus the divine name. Confirm; could say 'two words in Hebrew'.
